# The DER/X.509 parser against a reference parser, frozen.
#
# 17,118 mutated certificates -- every prefix of each fixture, single- and
# two-byte mutations biased toward the structural head, truncations,
# appended bytes, and splices between two certificates -- were fed to the
# reference parser and to this module, and the two verdicts recorded. This file is
# the part of that run worth keeping: every case where the two disagreed,
# plus 1,100 where they agreed, chosen shortest-first so the corpus stays
# small.
#
# The oracle is no longer available, so the corpus cannot be regenerated.
#
# <certificate as hex> <1 if the reference accepted> <1 if x509 accepted>
#
# A line whose two columns differ is a *decision*, not a defect, and there are
# two kinds.
#
# x509 stricter than the reference (73 in the full run). DER's encoding rules enforced
# where the reference parser is content: trailing bytes inside a structure, a
# non-minimal integer, a tag where another was required. Being stricter than
# the oracle, in a parser reading what an attacker sent, is the safe direction
# to differ in.
#
# x509 looser than the reference (54 in the full run), and all 54 are one thing: a
# malformed *extension this module does not interpret* -- subject and
# authority key identifiers, certificate policies, policy mappings, authority
# information access, CRL distribution points. The reference parses those and errors;
# this module carries them as bytes and never reads them, and RFC 5280 4.2
# permits ignoring a non-critical extension. Nothing is ignored here that
# anything acts on: an unrecognized extension marked *critical* is recorded
# and makes verification fail, which tests/x509_test.nio asserts separately.
# If any of those five ever starts being interpreted, it must be parsed
# strictly at the same time, and this paragraph is where that is written down.
